body:
Revenue from land held under direct administration

Administration needed dependable income to pay soldiers, maintain forts and run the kingdom. Shivaji strengthened land measurement and assessment and tried to reduce reliance on intermediaries who could retain revenue or build their own armed following. In important settlements, land was measured with a kathi or measuring rod, crop output was estimated and officials supervised collection. Annaji Datto is associated with major revenue-survey arrangements.

A commonly described assessment divided the estimated agricultural produce into 3 shares for the cultivator and 2 for the state out of 5—approximately 40% for the state. This is a description of a revenue settlement, not proof that every field in every season yielded an identical payment. In practice, revenue could be collected in cash or in kind, with local conditions affecting collections.

Claims on areas outside direct swarajya

Two terms frequently occur together but mean different things. Chauth literally denotes a fourth and was a claim generally expressed as 25% of assessed land revenue in territories from which the Marathas demanded tribute, often in return for refraining from raids. Sardeshmukhi was an additional claim of roughly 9–10% of land revenue, associated with the superior revenue-collecting right of a sardeshmukh.

Revenue conceptBasisRemember
Land revenue in swarajyaAssessment of cultivated land and estimated produceA settlement often described as about 2/5 of produce for the state.
ChauthClaim on revenue of a territory subject to Maratha tribute1/4, or 25%.
SardeshmukhiAdditional superior-revenue claimAbout 9–10%.

The 40% land-assessment description concerns production on assessed lands. In contrast, 25% and 9–10% describe separate levies on the assessed revenue of territories under a Maratha claim. They are not 3 interchangeable rates on the same individual peasant's crop, nor should all be combined to produce a universal tax rate. Later, as the Marathas expanded, rights to chauth and sardeshmukhi became important sources of income and political influence for the Chhatrapati, the Peshwa and individual chiefs.

If a tributary territory's assessed land revenue was 100 units, a chauth claim at 25% would equal 25 units, and a separate sardeshmukhi claim at 10% would equal 10 units. This numerical illustration does not make those levies identical to the swarajya land settlement.

Prelims focus

  • Kathi: rod used in land measurement.
  • Annaji Datto: important figure in Shivaji's revenue settlement.
  • Land assessment: often described as 2/5 of estimated produce for the state.
  • Chauth: 25% of assessed land revenue; sardeshmukhi: about 9–10% as an additional claim.
  • Trap: chauth and sardeshmukhi are not the same as ordinary produce assessment within directly administered swarajya.

[IGNOU, History of Bharat, BHIM-162, Unit 7, § 7.3, “Revenue System in Maratha State (17th Century)” (consulted 19 November 2026); NCERT, Our Pasts – II, Class 7, Chapter 10, printed p. 150; Maharashtra State Gazetteer, History, Part III: Maratha Period, Chapter 1, discussion of tribute outside swarajya (consulted 19 November 2026).]

pictures.alt: Estimated produce splits 40% to the state and 60% to cultivators; assessed revenue is the separate base for chauth at 25% and sardeshmukhi at about 9–10%.
pictures.caption: These shares refer to different revenue bases and should not be added indiscriminately.

title: Maratha Land Revenue, Chauth and Sardeshmukhi

body:
Why forts were central to Shivaji's strategy

Shivaji's military system was adapted to the hill country of the western Deccan. A network of forts protected passes, stored provisions, sheltered troops and provided defensible positions from which mobile forces could operate. Raigad served as a royal centre and the site of Shivaji's coronation in 1674; Pratapgad is associated with the confrontation with Afzal Khan in 1659. These were inland strongholds, whereas Sindhudurg and Vijaydurg were associated with the western coast and maritime defence.

A fort was not supposed to depend entirely on the unchecked decision of 1 officer. The havaldar supervised the fort and its keys, the sabnis maintained records and correspondence, the sarnobat commanded the garrison, and the karkhanis looked after stores and supplies. Divided responsibility made it harder for one commander to misuse a strategically important stronghold.

Fast movement and cavalry distinctions

The army combined infantry familiar with the passes and light cavalry capable of quick movement and attacks on an opponent's communications. Such methods are often called guerrilla warfare or ganimi kava: small mobile units use terrain, surprise and speed instead of depending only on battles between large armies. The term describes methods, not a separate branch of government.

Two cavalry terms are useful: a bargir received a horse and equipment from the state, whereas a silhedar generally provided his own horse and equipment. This difference concerns who equipped the horseman, not which community he belonged to.

Why a navy was also necessary

The Konkan coastline required defence against threats by sea as well as by land. Shivaji developed naval forces and strengthened coastal positions to contest control of routes and ports where Portuguese, Siddis of Janjira and other maritime powers were active. Naval vessels included ghurabs (armed vessels or gunboats) and galivats (smaller rowing-and-sailing vessels). The navy complemented the forts; it did not replace the inland army.

Prelims focus

  • Raigad: Shivaji's coronation site, 1674; Pratapgad: Afzal Khan episode, 1659.
  • Sindhudurg and Vijaydurg: important coastal forts.
  • Havaldar: fort supervision; sabnis: records; sarnobat: garrison; karkhanis: supplies.
  • Bargir: state-equipped cavalryman; silhedar: self-equipped cavalryman.
  • Ghurab: armed naval vessel; galivat: rowing-and-sailing craft.

[IGNOU, Rise of the Marathas in the 17th Century, Unit 10, §§ 10.8.3–10.8.4; IGNOU, Rise of Marathas: Shivaji Maharaj, Unit 15, §§ 15.4–15.4.1; Maharashtra State Gazetteer, History, Part III: Maratha Period, Chapter 1, military organisation and forts (all consulted 19 November 2026).]

pictures.alt: Sailors load supplies onto wooden Maratha sailing and rowing vessels beside a Konkan coastal stone fort overlooking the Arabian Sea.
pictures.caption: Coastal forts and vessels supported Maratha control along the Konkan.

pictures.alt: Four officers share fort duties: havaldar supervises and holds keys, sabnis keeps records, sarnobat commands the garrison, and karkhanis manages supplies.
pictures.caption: Shared duties protected a fort against military and administrative failure.

title: Forts, Mobile Forces and the Maratha Navy

body:
From Shivaji's successors to a powerful chief minister

The Maratha state continued after Shivaji died in 1680. Sambhaji, followed by Rajaram and the leadership of Tarabai, sustained resistance during Aurangzeb's Deccan campaigns. After Aurangzeb's death in 1707, Shahu emerged as an important Chhatrapati. In this setting the Peshwa, originally the principal minister serving the ruler, became increasingly powerful.

Balaji Vishwanath became Peshwa under Shahu in 1713. In 1719, Mughal imperial orders confirmed Maratha claims to chauth and sardeshmukhi from the 6 Deccan provinces. These claims meant access to revenue and recognition of political influence, not direct day-to-day administration of every place that owed tribute.

Major Peshwas and events

PeshwaPeriodMain association
Balaji Vishwanath1713–1720Strengthened Shahu's position; secured imperial recognition of revenue claims in 1719.
Baji Rao I1720–1740Mobile campaigns in Malwa, Gujarat and north India; defeated the Nizam at Palkhed (1728); Maratha raid on Delhi (1737).
Balaji Baji Rao (Nana Saheb)1740–1761Wider territorial and tributary expansion; period ends with the major setback at Panipat (1761).

How Peshwa expansion worked

Under Baji Rao I, Maratha forces often avoided direct assaults on the strongest Mughal fortifications. They moved rapidly, raided centres of wealth and attacked where an enemy's reinforcements were difficult to bring. This increased pressure on Mughal provincial authority. By the 1720s and 1730s, Maratha influence was spreading across Malwa and Gujarat, while rights to collect tribute grew in the Deccan. The raid on Delhi in 1737 signalled the weakness of imperial defence, although a successful raid was not the same as permanent annexation of the capital.

The Chhatrapati remained the royal title, associated with the Satara court, while the Peshwa at Pune increasingly directed military campaigns and administration. Powerful sardars commanded their own forces and controlled growing regional interests. This arrangement is often described as the Maratha Confederacy: major chiefs were linked by a common Maratha political order but did not always act as a single centrally controlled army.

Prelims focus

  • Balaji Vishwanath: Peshwa from 1713; imperial revenue grants in 1719.
  • Baji Rao I: Peshwa 1720–1740; Palkhed 1728; Delhi raid 1737.
  • Balaji Baji Rao: also called Nana Saheb; Peshwa 1740–1761.
  • Pune: Peshwa power centre; Satara: associated with the Chhatrapati.
  • Trap: a Peshwa was a chief minister by title, not the same office as the Chhatrapati.

[NCERT, Our Pasts – II, Class 7, Chapter 10, printed pp. 149–151; IGNOU, The Maratha State System, Block 1, § 3.3, “The Maratha Confederacy”, and § 3.3.1, “The King and the Peshwa”; IGNOU, Regional Kingdoms, Unit 18, § 18.4.3, “Maratha Confederacy and the Peshwas” (online sources consulted 19 November 2026).]

pictures.caption: Trace how the Peshwa's office and Maratha territorial ambitions expanded.

title: The Rise of the Peshwas and Maratha Expansion to 1761

body:
Territory ruled directly and territory paying tribute

Maratha influence in the eighteenth century stretched far beyond Shivaji's original western Deccan kingdom. Some territories came under the sustained administration of Maratha chiefs, while other rulers paid chauth, sardeshmukhi or other tribute without being absorbed into a single directly governed state. A military expedition, a revenue claim and permanent territorial control are therefore different forms of political power.

Identify the leading Maratha houses

Maratha housePrincipal centreRegional association
GaekwadBaroda (Vadodara)Gujarat
Sindhia (Shinde)GwaliorCentral India; also associated with Ujjain
HolkarIndoreMalwa
BhonsleNagpurCentral India and eastern campaigns

Gujarat connection: Maratha pressure expanded into Gujarat during the Peshwa period, but control developed over years rather than by a single conquest of the whole province. The Gujarat government's Vadodara district history associates Pilaji Rao Gaekwad with the capture of Songadh in 1726 and the expansion of Maratha authority in south Gujarat. Damaji Rao Gaekwad then consolidated the Gaekwad hold over Baroda in the 1730s. This rise of the Gaekwads is distinct from Shivaji's earlier 1664 raid on Surat.

Panipat: the limit to rapid northern expansion

During the Peshwa period, Maratha armies campaigned into Rajasthan and the Punjab, as well as eastern and southern regions. But campaigns and tribute demands also generated opposition among regional rulers. In northern India the Marathas faced the Afghan ruler Ahmad Shah Abdali (Durrani). On 14 January 1761, the Third Battle of Panipat was fought between the Marathas, whose principal field commander was Sadashivrao Bhau, and Abdali's forces and allies. The Marathas suffered a severe defeat.

The defeat checked their immediate ambition to dominate north India and exposed the problems created by extended campaigns and insufficient local support. It did not immediately abolish Maratha power: the Peshwa's authority and the regional Maratha houses continued after 1761. The battle should also not be confused with a war against the British East India Company, which was not the opposing force at Panipat.

Prelims focus

  • Gaekwad — Baroda/Vadodara; Sindhia — Gwalior; Holkar — Indore; Bhonsle — Nagpur.
  • 1726 — Pilaji Gaekwad — Songadh; 1730s — Gaekwad consolidation at Baroda.
  • 1664 Surat raid and eighteenth-century Gaekwad rule are different events.
  • 14 January 1761: Third Battle of Panipat; Marathas versus Ahmad Shah Abdali.
  • Sadashivrao Bhau: principal Maratha field commander at Panipat.
  • Trap: tribute-paying regions were not all directly annexed; defeat at Panipat did not end Maratha political existence.

[NCERT, Our Pasts – II, Class 7, Chapter 10, printed pp. 149–151; NCERT, Our Pasts – III, Class 8, Chapter 2, “From Trade to Territory”, printed p. 18, 2020–21 edition; Government of Gujarat, Vadodara District Administration, “History”, Gaekwad section (consulted 19 November 2026); IGNOU, History of India from the Mid-Eighteenth Century, BHIC-110, discussion of the Third Battle of Panipat (consulted 19 November 2026).]

pictures.caption: The connected developments, from Shivaji's state to the regional powers of 1761.
